Subject to any international management / trade controls

documentation.range: This cactus has been reported from the Mexican state of Durango in the Corneto Pass area, at an altitude of 2,150 to 2,300 m asl (Pilbeam 1999). W.A. and B. Fitz Maurice (pers. comm. 2009) know it only from two sites about five kilometres apart. Hunt et al. (2006) say it is only known from the type locality.
documentation.population: The population is small, certainly not much more than 200 individuals.
documentation.habitats: This cactus is found growing on rocky limestone outcrops (Pilbeam 1999), in grassland with nearby pine-oak forest.
documentation.threats: Illegal collection and road construction pose threats to this species.
documentation.measures:
The species is legally protected in Mexico by the national list of species at risk of extinction, NOM-059-SEMARNAT-2010, where it is listed under the category “threatened” (A; SEMARNAT 2010).

This species does not occur in any protected area.
documentation.use_trade: This cactus is popular with collectors as an ornamental plant. The species has been seized in Mexico and the Netherlands (Bárcenas 2003).
documentation.rationale: Mammillaria theresae has a very small range (the extent of occurrence is possibly as low as 25 km²), it is known essentially from one location, and there is a continuing decline in mature individuals due to illegal collection. Many collection records are cited in Pilbeam (1999), all from the same locality, which underlines the heavy pressure on this small population. Hence, it is listed as Critically Endangered.
